title: PPE, hygiene and exposure escalation
audience: Cleaners who may be exposed to chemicals and must recognise and escalate exposure symptoms.
learningOutcomes: Recognise exposure symptoms and follow the site's emergency and escalation route.
Refuse to use an unidentified agent or an unknown glove type.
Record the exposure concern and refer it through the site response route.

instruction.heading: How degreasing chemicals reach the body
instruction.body: Industrial degreasers include solvents, alkaline cleaners, emulsifiers and water-based products, and each carries its own hazards. Exposure can happen through the skin, through the eyes, by breathing vapour or mist, and, less often, by swallowing material that has been carried on the hands. Splashes during pouring or spraying, soaked rags, and open containers in a warm or poorly ventilated area all increase the chance of contact. The safety data sheet for each product is the main source of information. It describes the health effects, the hazardous ingredients, safe handling and storage, emergency procedures and first aid, and the PPE that the supplier recommends. The Safe Work Australia code on managing hazardous chemicals says that the current SDS should be readily accessible to the workers who use the chemical, and near the work area. If you cannot find the SDS for a product in front of you, you do not have the information you need to start work with it.

instruction.heading: Recognising exposure
instruction.body: Symptoms depend on the product and the route of exposure. Skin contact can cause dryness, cracking, redness, burning or a rash. Eye contact can cause stinging, watering, blurred vision or more serious damage. Breathing vapour can cause headache, dizziness, nausea, a sore throat or cough, or a feeling of being unwell. Some effects appear later, which is why a person who feels fine after a splash should still report it. Do not decide for yourself that a symptom is trivial, and do not wait to see whether it passes. Know the site's emergency route, the first-aid contact and the location of the eyewash and first-aid kit before you begin any task. Follow the first-aid section of the SDS for the product you were using, and follow the site's emergency policy.

instruction.heading: PPE chosen from the SDS, not from habit
instruction.body: PPE is the last line of protection, not the first. The Safe Work Australia code ranks controls so that elimination, substitution, isolation and engineering controls come before administrative controls, and PPE comes last, to be relied on mainly where higher controls are not yet in place or are not enough. In practice, that means ventilation, enclosure and a safer product should be considered before a glove is chosen. Where PPE is needed, it must suit the product. The code says gloves should be chosen for the best resistance to the chemical in use, because some gloves resist some solvents and fail with others. It also notes that the SDS and the product label may specify PPE, for example a particular glove material for hydrocarbon or chlorinated solvents. Choose the glove the SDS or the site procedure names, check it for damage before use, and replace it when it is torn, swollen or contaminated. Eye protection and face protection are chosen the same way, from the SDS and the task. If you are offered an unknown glove for an unidentified agent, refuse it, ask for the SDS and the approved PPE, and record the request.

instruction.heading: Hygiene that protects you and others
instruction.body: Hygiene reduces the chance of carrying residue away from the work area. Remove contaminated PPE before you leave the work area and store it where the site requires. Do not wear degreasing gloves or overalls into a break room, a canteen or a vehicle. Wash your hands and face before eating, drinking or smoking, and do not eat or drink in the degreasing area. Launder contaminated work clothing separately, as the site procedure states, and do not take it home with other laundry. Keep disposable PPE in a closed bin, not on the floor. If you handle rags or absorbents that have been used with a product, treat them as contaminated until the SDS and the site procedure say otherwise. These habits are simple, but they are the ones most often missed, and they matter most at the end of a long shift.

instruction.heading: Escalating a possible exposure
instruction.body: If you or a colleague may have been exposed, stop the task at once and move away from the source, using the route the procedure sets out. Follow the emergency route and the first-aid section of the SDS. Tell the named supervisor immediately, and make sure the person affected is seen by the first-aid contact. Record the time, the product if it is known, the route of exposure if it is known, the symptoms, the first aid given, and the people informed. Keep the product container or its label, if it can be done safely, so that the product can be identified. Do not return to the area to finish the task until the supervisor has confirmed that the area is safe and the controls have been checked. The site's incident procedure governs what happens next, and the report is made whether or not the symptoms seem minor.

instruction.heading: Register, records and health monitoring
instruction.body: A site that uses hazardous chemicals must keep a register of them, and each chemical on the register must have a current SDS. The Safe Work Australia code says the register should be kept at the workplace, be readily accessible to workers and others who may be affected, and be kept up to date, with an SDS that is no more than five years old. Health monitoring is a separate duty, which applies to some exposures and not others. A site's occupational health advice, or the advice of the person who holds the monitoring duty, decides whether monitoring is needed.

procedure: Before starting, locate the SDS for each product, confirm the emergency route, the first-aid contact, the eyewash and the first-aid kit.
Check the PPE the SDS and the site procedure name, and inspect each item before use.
Refuse any unidentified agent or unknown glove type, and ask for the SDS and approved PPE.
Keep PPE and contaminated rags contained in the work area, and wash before eating, drinking or smoking.
If exposure is possible, stop, move away from the source and follow the emergency route and the SDS first-aid section.
Tell the named supervisor at once, and make sure the affected person is seen by the first-aid contact.
Record the time, product, route, symptoms, first aid given and people informed, and do not resume until the supervisor confirms the area is safe.

workedExamples.situation: A cleaner is offered a pair of unfamiliar gloves for an agent whose label has been rubbed off. (Example scenario; the product is fictional.)
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What do you do before any work starts?
workedExamples.reasoning: Refuse to start. The agent is unidentified and the glove is unknown, so the protection cannot be confirmed. Ask for the SDS for the product and for the PPE it names, and check the glove material against the SDS. Record the request, the time and who was asked. Work does not begin until the product is identified and the PPE is confirmed by the site.

workedExamples.situation: A cleaner splashes a degreaser onto the forearm and the sleeve becomes wet through. The cleaner says it is only a little and wants to finish the bay. (Example scenario.)
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the sequence of actions?
workedExamples.reasoning: Stop the task and move away from the source. Remove the contaminated clothing and follow the first-aid section of the SDS for that product, and tell the named supervisor at once so that the first-aid contact can assess the cleaner. Record the time, product, route, symptoms and first aid given. Do not finish the bay until the supervisor has confirmed that the area and the controls have been checked. Saying it was only a little is not a reason to continue.

workedExamples.situation: In a poorly ventilated pit, a cleaner develops a headache and dizziness after an hour of degreasing with an open container nearby. A colleague suggests opening the door and carrying on. (Example scenario.)
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Is it acceptable to continue once the door is open?
workedExamples.reasoning: No. Leave the area and tell the supervisor. Symptoms during degreasing in a poorly ventilated space are a possible exposure and a warning about the controls, not a ventilation problem to solve on the spot. Do not re-enter until a competent person has checked the controls and the supervisor has confirmed that the area is safe. If the space is a confined space, it cannot be entered without a permit under the confined spaces code. Record the symptoms, the time and the controls observed.

equipmentAndPpe: SDS for each product in use, kept at the work area and readily accessible.
Gloves chosen for the product named on the SDS, inspected before use.
Eye protection, and face protection where the SDS or task requires it.
Closed footwear and clothing as set by the site procedure, with contaminated items kept separate.
Eyewash and first-aid kit located and checked before work begins.
Emergency contact card with the first-aid contact, the supervisor and the site emergency route.
Respiratory protection only where the site assessment calls for it, selected and fitted under the site program; this lesson does not choose it.
Closed bin for contaminated disposable PPE and rags.

commonErrors.prevention: Match the glove to the material named on the SDS, and inspect it before use.

commonErrors.error: Waiting to see whether symptoms pass.
commonErrors.prevention: Stop, leave the area, tell the supervisor, and follow the emergency route.

commonErrors.error: Carrying contaminated gloves or overalls to the break room.
commonErrors.prevention: Remove and store contaminated PPE in the work area, and wash before eating or drinking.

commonErrors.error: Continuing to work because the air has been improved by opening a door.
commonErrors.prevention: Leave the area after symptoms, and do not re-enter until a competent person confirms the controls.

commonErrors.error: Treating PPE as the first control, and skipping ventilation or product selection.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the higher controls first, then choose PPE from the SDS.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Under the Safe Work Australia code on managing hazardous chemicals (dated July 2012 as shown in the document), the current SDS for each chemical must be readily accessible to the workers who use it, and it covers health effects, emergency procedures and safe handling.
The same code ranks PPE last among control measures and says gloves should be chosen for resistance to the chemical in use. The SDS or label may specify the PPE to use.

The Safe Work Australia register guidance (page showing 2011 as the model law date; no publication date) says that a register of hazardous chemicals must be kept at the workplace, be readily accessible, be kept up to date, and include a current SDS for each listed chemical.

This lesson does not authorise handling of any hazardous chemical beyond the site's approved tasks, and does not grant a licence, certificate, competence or health clearance. Completing it does not make a cleaner a chemical specialist or a health professional.

qualityStandard: Emergency route, first-aid contact, eyewash and first-aid kit identified before the simulated task.
Unidentified agent and unknown glove refused, and the SDS requested, in the case study.
Exposure escalation completed in the role-play: stop, leave the source, tell the supervisor, and record the time, product, symptoms and first aid.
Contaminated PPE shown to be kept in the work area, not carried to the break room.
documentationEvidence: Exposure concern record with time, product, route if known, symptoms, first aid given and people informed.
PPE check record matched to the SDS for the named product.
Register check showing that each product in use has a current SDS available at the work area.
summary: Know the emergency route, the first-aid contact and the SDS before starting.
Choose PPE from the SDS, after higher controls, and refuse unidentified agents or unknown gloves.
On possible exposure, stop, leave, tell the supervisor, follow the SDS first aid, and record it.

knowledgeChecks.question: You are offered an unknown glove for an unidentified agent. What is correct?
options: Use it, to be safe, since it is the only glove on hand
Refuse, and ask for the SDS and the approved PPE
Use two gloves of different types, one over the other

knowledgeChecks.question: You may have been exposed to a chemical and feel unwell. What do you do?
options: Stop, move away, tell the supervisor, and follow the emergency route
Wait to see whether it passes, since most symptoms settle down
Finish the task first, then tell the supervisor at the end

knowledgeChecks.question: Where should contaminated PPE be removed and stored?
options: In the break room, before eating
On the way home, in the car
In the work area, before leaving it
